At the gram panchayat office in Yavatmal district, Tejas slapped the yield register on the table. "Look. The six villages that got solar pumps last year harvested far more cotton. The pumps did it."
Vinita, the block's agriculture officer, turned the pages slowly. "Maybe. But which villages got pumps first?"
"The ones that applied fast."
"The ones whose sarpanches know the paperwork, where farmers already had some money. They might have done better anyway. Or did the farmers who were already doing well put in extra for the pumps?" She tapped the rainfall column. "And the eastern side got more rain this year. That's where most pumps are."
Tejas frowned. "So the pumps did nothing?"
"I didn't say that. Find me six similar villages without pumps, same rain, same size farms, and we compare. Then we'll know what to tell the collector."

qa.q: What does the yield register show, according to Tejas?
qa.a: The six villages that got solar pumps last year harvested far more cotton.

qa.q: What is Vinita thinking when she asks which villages got pumps first?
qa.a: Vinita feels doubtful about the claim, suspecting those villages were different to begin with, with better paperwork and more money, so their good harvest might not be the pumps' doing.

qa.q: What comparison does Vinita ask for, and why does it help?
qa.a: Six similar villages without pumps, with the same rain and farm size; comparing them separates the pumps' effect from rain and money.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when Vinita questions the finding?
qa.a: Tejas might feel the good news is being brushed aside at first, though Vinita makes clear she isn't saying the pumps did nothing.

grounding: It shows an officer asking about third causes, reverse direction and rainfall, and asking for a comparison group before crediting the pumps.

"Customers with the loyalty app spend forty percent more," Kofi announced, pointing at the chart on the big screen in the Rotterdam office. "Let's push the app harder and watch sales climb."
Santiago leaned back. "Or the people who already spend a lot are exactly the ones who bother to download it. That runs the arrow the other way."
"Hm."
"And most of these downloads came in December. Everyone spends more in December." He scrolled. "Also, app users live closer to our shops. Distance could drive both."
Kofi crossed his arms. "So what would convince you?"
"Send the app invite to a random half of new customers next month, and not to the other half. If the invited half spend more, I'm on your side."
Kofi sighed, then grinned. "Fine. Random half it is."

qa.q: What figure did Kofi announce about app customers?
qa.a: Customers with the loyalty app spend forty percent more.

qa.q: Why does Santiago doubt that the app is what makes people spend more?
qa.a: He suspects big spenders are simply the ones who download it, that December inflated spending, and that living near the shops could drive both.

qa.q: What test does Santiago propose, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Invite a random half of new customers and not the other half; since chance decides who gets the invite, a spending gap would point to the app itself. 👍

qa.q: What would change if the invited half spent no more than the others?
qa.a: The team would learn the link came from who downloads the app, not from the app, and could stop spending effort pushing it.

grounding: It shows an analyst raising reverse direction, a third cause and timing coincidence, and proposing a random comparison group before claiming cause.

The monthly meeting at the women's hostel ran late, and Tenzin had one last slide. "Residents who come to morning yoga took far fewer sick days this term. I think we should make it compulsory."
Nirmala, the welfare officer, looked at the list of names. "Before we decide, can I ask a few things? Who comes to yoga at six? People who already sleep early and feel well. Someone with a cold isn't getting up for it. So feeling well might bring people to yoga, not only the other way round."
Tenzin nodded slowly.
"And the yoga group is mostly final-years with fewer late labs. That could matter too." She pulled up a blank sheet. "Could we compare residents with similar timetables, some who start yoga next month and some who don't, and look again at the end of term?"

qa.q: What did Tenzin want to make compulsory?
qa.a: Morning yoga.

qa.q: What is Nirmala thinking when she says someone with a cold isn't getting up for it?
qa.a: Nirmala feels doubtful about the slide, suspecting the link runs backwards: residents who already feel well are the ones who come, so fewer sick days might not be the yoga's doing.

qa.q: Why is Nirmala's suggested comparison better than deciding now?
qa.a: Comparing residents with similar timetables, some starting yoga and some not, removes the timetable and early-sleeper differences, so any gap is more likely due to yoga.

qa.q: How might residents feel if yoga became compulsory because of this slide?
qa.a: Some might resent being pulled out of bed at six for a benefit nobody has shown, especially those with late labs.

grounding: It shows an officer checking for reverse direction and a hidden third factor and proposing a fair comparison before making a rule.

passage:
Subject: Smart boards and results, before we send the funders' report

Hi Ira,
I know the draft says the smart boards "raised Class 8 scores by 14 marks". The link is real in the data. I'm just not ready to say the boards caused it, and I'd like one more week.
Three things are bothering me. First, the twelve schools that got boards are mostly in the ward with more teachers per class. That alone could explain better scores. Second, the direction: the district gave boards first to schools that were already doing well, as a reward. Third, it's one year of results, and one year can swing by chance.
What I'd like to do is compare them with the eight schools on the waiting list that look most like them, same ward, same teacher numbers, same scores two years ago. If the gap holds there, I'll sign the sentence happily.
Aadhya

qa.q: How many schools on the waiting list does Aadhya want to compare with?
qa.a: The eight schools on the waiting list that look most like the board schools.

qa.q: What is Aadhya worried about if the report goes out as drafted?
qa.a: Aadhya is worried the report will claim the boards caused the higher scores when more teachers, the district rewarding strong schools, or a lucky year could explain the link.

qa.q: Which step in Aadhya's plan is the strongest, and why?
qa.a: Comparing with the most similar waiting-list schools, because it shows what scores looked like without boards, so any gap left is more likely due to the boards.

qa.q: How might Ira feel reading this email just before the funders' report?
qa.a: Ira may feel a bit frustrated by the delay but also relieved that a claim the funders might check has been tested before it goes out.

grounding: It shows a careful analyst asking whether a third cause, reverse direction or chance explains a link, and seeking a comparison group before claiming cause.

passage:
Jyoti, you asked on the show what I actually do at the academy. Okay, here's one story.
Last season the head coach showed me a chart. Players who did the new video sessions improved their batting average far more than players who didn't. He wanted to make them compulsory and buy three more cameras.
I'm the analyst, so my first question was, who chose which players went to the video sessions? Turns out the coaches picked the ones they thought were "about to break through". So the players were already rising. That's the direction problem.
Then I asked what else those players had. Extra net time, as it happened. Third cause.
So we ran it properly. Next term, among players the coaches rated the same, half got video sessions by draw and half didn't. The video group did improve, a little. Much less than the chart. We bought one camera, not three.
Ankita, analyst. That's the job.

qa.q: How many cameras did the academy finally buy?
qa.a: One camera, not three.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel about the head coach's chart at first, and why?
qa.a: Ankita was sceptical, suspecting the chart looked better than the truth because coaches had picked players who were already rising and those players also had extra net time.

qa.q: Which choice made Ankita's approach convincing, and why?
qa.a: Splitting similarly rated players by draw into video and no-video groups; it removed the coaches' choices and the extra net time as explanations, so the small real effect could be seen.

qa.q: How might the head coach have felt when the proper test showed a much smaller gain?
qa.a: The head coach might have been disappointed after hoping for a big win, but also better placed to spend money on what actually helps players.

grounding: It shows a careful analyst checking reverse direction and a third cause, then using a fair comparison group before claiming the video sessions helped.
